[ὥς] φησι Φιλοστόργιος Ἰώσηπον Ἰοῦστον; τὰ κατὰ Τοὐναντίον μὲν οὖν ὁ Ἰώ- ον. Ὅτι τά ἄλλα καὶ ὅσα πρὸς ἱστορίας ἥκει λόγον Φιλο- στόργιος τὸν Παμφίλου Εὐσέβιον ἐπαινῶν, περὶ τὴν εὐσέβειαν διαμαρ- τάνειν φησί. καὶ τὸ ἁμάρτημα ὁ δυσσεβὴς διηγούμενος, διότι ἄγνω- στον τὸ ϑεῖον καὶ ἀκατάληπτον ἡγοῖτο, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄλλα τοιαῦτά φησιν αὐτὸν πλημμελεῖν. καταπαῦσαι δὲ αὐτὸν τὰς οἰκείας τῆς ἷστο- ρίας μνήμας μέχρι τῆς τῶν παίδων διαδοχῆς τοῦ μεγάλου Κωνσταν- τίνου συνεπιμαρτύρεται. thought_title: Judging old histories and how the quarrel over Alexander and Arius and Constantine began
orientation: Philostorgius is speaking in his own narrative voice, first judging Jewish and church histories and then tracing the Arian quarrel to Alexander Baucalis and recording the succession from Constantius to Constantine.
pass_a_gloss: That concerning the books of Maccabees he says that whoever he is he does not know. Yet the first book he deems worthy of acceptance, as reporting things in agreement with the prophecies of Daniel, and because it goes through very providently how the toil of men drove the affairs of the Jews to the extreme of evils, and how again the virtue of men brought them up, and then they took back power against their enemies and the temple was cleansed from Greek pollutions. But the second he says does not show the same author. But it is an abridgment of the things recorded by Jason of Cyrene in five books, which announces the war which Judas Maccabeus warred against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son called Eupator. But the third he rejects. Calling it monstrous and going through nothing like the first. But the fourth, he himself agreeing that it was written by Josephus, he says it is not history rather than praise, reporting the things concerning Eleazar and the seven sons, the Maccabees. Of this Phlegon, as Philostorgius says, as far as to have gone at greater length through the breadth of the things that befell the Jews, with Phlegon and Dion having briefly mentioned them and having made them a parenthesis of their own narrative. Since not even this man is shown to have cared at all for the things that draw toward piety and the other virtue, in the same manner as not even those men. But on the contrary Josephus both seems like one who feared and one who was cautious lest he offend Greeks. As Philostorgius says concerning Josephus and Justus, the things concerning ... [text damaged and broken here]. That in other things and in as many things as pertain to history Philostorgius praising Eusebius associate of Pamphilus, says he misses concerning piety. And explaining the error as an ungodly man, because he held the divine to be unknown and ungraspable, and he says he also errs in other such things. And he testifies with him that he ended his own memorials of history as far as the succession of the sons of Constantine the Great. That this ungodly man says that the votes for the bishopric while being cast for Arius, he himself having preferred Alexander above himself, contrived that these should pass over to him. That a certain Alexander a presbyter called Baucalis by nickname, because the mass of overnourished flesh heaped up under his rear parts imitated the shape of an earthen jar, which things they are accustomed to call baukala by local custom, this man he says holding second rank began the cause from which the strife broke out between Alexander the bishop and Arius. And the proclamation of same substance was contrived from there. That, he says, Constantius, the father of Constantine the Great, for manly worth of the upper Galatias, in which are also the called Alps, was shown forth as emperor. And these places are hard to enter and hard to approach. And the Galatias those now call Gallias. And the end of Constantius happened at the place called Iluion. In which also Constantine his son finding him sick, having fled in marvelous manner the plot of Diocletian, buried him dying, and became successor of the emperorship. That the change of Constantine the Great from Greek religion to Christianity even this man agreeing with the others records that the cause was the victory over Daxentius. Which [sentence breaks off, text ends].

pass_b_english: Philostorgius says he does not know who wrote the books of Maccabees, whoever it was. He approves the first book, since it agrees with the prophecies of Daniel. It also recounts very thoughtfully how the wickedness of men drove Jewish affairs to the depth of evils, and how the courage of men raised them again. Then they won back power over their enemies, and the temple was cleansed from Greek defilements. He says the second book shows a different writer, for it is an abridgment of the five volumes written by Jason of Cyrene. That work recounts the war which Judas Maccabeus waged against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son surnamed Eupator. He rejects the third book, calling it monstrous and wholly unlike the first. He too agrees that Josephus wrote the fourth, but he says it is less a history than a speech of praise, telling the story of Eleazar and the seven Maccabean children.

Philostorgius says Josephus differs from this Phlegon only in treating the events that befell the Jews at greater length, although Phlegon and Dion mentioned them only briefly and made them a parenthesis in their own narrative. For he shows no concern at all for matters that lead to piety and the rest of virtue, and they showed none either. Josephus, on the contrary, seems both fearful and cautious, lest he offend the Greeks.

Philostorgius praises Eusebius, the associate of Pamphilus, in everything else that belongs to history, but he says he went wrong concerning piety. This impious man explains the fault by saying that he held the divine to be unknown and incomprehensible, and that he committed other such errors. He adds that Eusebius closed the record of his history at the succession of the sons of Constantine the Great.

This impious man says the votes for the bishopric were falling to Arius, yet Arius preferred Alexander to himself and contrived to bring them round to him. Philostorgius speaks of a certain presbyter named Alexander Baucalis, so nicknamed because the mass of his overgrown flesh heaped on his upper back took the shape of an earthen jar, which people of the country commonly call baukala. He says this man held second rank and made the beginning of the cause from which the quarrel between Alexander the bishop and Arius broke out. The proclamation of same substance was contrived from that beginning.

Philostorgius says Constantius, the father of Constantine the Great, was appointed emperor over Upper Galatia for his valor, the land in which the so-called Alps lie. Those places are hard to invade and hard to enter, and men today call the Galatias the Gallias. The death of Constantius occurred in the land called Albion. His son Constantine found him sick there, after unexpectedly escaping the plot of Diocletian, and he buried him at his death and became successor to the emperorship.

Philostorgius agrees with the other writers that the change of Constantine the Great from Greek religion to Christianity came about through his victory over Daxentius. He records that victory as the cause.

problems.quote: Philostorgius says this Phlegon treated the events that befell the Jews at considerable length
problems.source_quote: Τούτου τοῦ Φλέγοντος, ὥς φησι φΦιλοστόργιος. ᾿ὕσον τὰ κατὰ τοὺς ᾿Ιουδαίους συμπεσόντα διὰ πλείο- νὸς ἐπεξελϑεῖν τοῦ πλάτους
problems.why: Misreads genitive "Τούτου τοῦ Φλέγοντος" as subject, making Phlegon contradict himself instead of contrasting Josephus with Phlegon and Dion, and drops "ὅσον" ("only insofar as").
problems.fix: Philostorgius says Josephus differs from this Phlegon only in treating the events that befell the Jews at greater length

problems.quote: yet Alexander preferred himself to Arius and contrived to bring them round to himself.
problems.source_quote: αὐτὸν μᾶλλον» ᾿Αλέξανδρον προτιμήσαντα ἑαυτοῦ, 1ὸ περιελϑεῖν αὐτῷ ταύτας καταπράξασϑαι.
problems.why: Reverses agency: in Greek, Arius preferred Alexander to himself and arranged for the votes to go to Alexander, not vice versa.
problems.fix: yet Arius preferred Alexander to himself and contrived to bring them round to him.
problems.ruling: αὐτὸν … προτιμήσαντα ἑαυτοῦ: Arius preferred Alexander, not Alexander preferring himself over Arius.

problems.quote: He explains the fault of the impious man
problems.source_quote: καὶ τὸ ἁμάρτημα ὁ δυσσεβὴς διηγούμενος
problems.why: Nominative "ὁ δυσσεβὴς" is the subject (Photius's slur for Philostorgius), not a genitive describing Eusebius as "the impious man".
problems.fix: This impious man explains the fault
problems.ruling: ὁ δυσσεβὴς διηγούμενος: nominative subject (Philostorgius), not Eusebius as 'the impious man'.

problems.source_quote: ὑπὸ τῶν μεταφρένων αὐτοῦ σε- σωρευμένον
problems.why: "μετάφρενα" means the upper back between the shoulders, not the buttocks.
problems.ruling: ὑπὸ τῶν μεταφρένων: μετάφρενα means upper back/shoulders, not buttocks.

problems.why: προμηθῶς means carefully, thoughtfully, or with foresight, not 'with great providence', which misleads the reader into thinking of divine providence.
problems.ruling: προμηθῶς is thoughtful care in narrative; 'providence' wrongly suggests divine πρόνοια, not diligent exposition.

problems.quote: He agrees that Josephus wrote the fourth as well
problems.source_quote: τὸ μέντοι τέταρτον ὑπὸ Ἰωσήπου γεγράρϑαι καὶ αὐτὸς συνομολογῶν
problems.why: καὶ αὐτὸς modifies συνομολογῶν ('he himself also agrees'), not 'the fourth'; the English wrongly implies Josephus also wrote another book of Maccabees.
problems.fix: He too agrees that Josephus wrote the fourth
problems.ruling: καὶ αὐτὸς συνομολογῶν is Philostorgius himself agreeing; 'Josephus…as well' misassigns also-writing to Josephus.

problems.quote: after escaping the plot of Diocletian by a sudden flight
problems.why: παραδόξως (OCR παραδύξος) means 'unexpectedly' or 'miraculously', not 'by a sudden flight', altering how Constantine's escape is described.
problems.fix: after unexpectedly escaping the plot of Diocletian
problems.ruling: παραδόξως (not sudden flight) qualifies escape unexpectedly; English duplicates φυγὼν and drops paradox.

last_rejected.quote: yet Arius preferred Alexander to himself and contrived to bring them round to him
last_rejected.source_quote: αὐτὸν μᾶλλον Ἀλέξανδρον προτιμήσαντα ἑαυτοῦ, τὸ περιελθεῖν αὐτῷ ταύτας καταπράξασθαι
last_rejected.why: Final "him" reads as Arius; Greek αὐτῷ is Alexander, whom Arius maneuvered the votes toward.
last_rejected.fix: yet Arius preferred Alexander to himself and contrived to bring the votes round to Alexander instead.
last_rejected.ruling: English mirrors Greek ἑαυτοῦ ('himself') vs. αὐτῷ ('him'); with subject Arius, non-reflexive 'him' clearly refers to Alexander, not Arius.
